nameStory: This little beetle gets its name from the two distinctive light-colored bands that stretch across its dark body, making it look like it's wearing a striped shirt. The 'Japanese' part of its name tells us where it originally came from before making its way to North America as an accidental stowaway.
description: The Two-banded Japanese Weevil is a small, dark beetle with a characteristic long snout that marks it as a member of the weevil family. Like all weevils, it has a distinctive elongated head that extends into a beak-like projection called a rostrum. These tiny beetles are part of the broad-nosed weevil group, meaning their snouts are shorter and wider than some of their needle-nosed cousins. They're small enough that you might mistake them for a piece of debris at first glance.

idTips.label: Two light bands
idTips.description: Look for two pale, cream-colored or yellowish bands that run across the dark brown or black body - this is the beetle's signature feature that gives it its name

idTips.label: Weevil snout
idTips.description: The head extends into a short, broad snout (rostrum) that's wider than a pencil lead, giving the beetle a distinctive pig-nosed appearance

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Tiny enough to sit comfortably on your thumbnail, these beetles are easily overlooked among garden debris

idTips.label: Hard wing covers
idTips.description: The wing covers feel firm and smooth to the touch, with a slightly glossy appearance that catches light

idTips.label: Elbowed antennae
idTips.description: The antennae have a distinct bend or elbow in them and end in a small club-like structure

habitat: You'll find these weevils in gardens, nurseries, and landscaped areas throughout New England, particularly where ornamental plants and shrubs are grown. They're especially common around rhododendrons, azaleas, and other broadleaf evergreens. Look for them on or near the soil surface around these plants, as both adults and larvae are associated with the root systems.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging to feed on plant roots and beginning their reproductive cycle. This is when you're most likely to spot them moving around on soil surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and larvae are developing in the soil. Adults may be found on plants during evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding to build up energy reserves before winter, though they become less active as temperatures drop. Late fall activity depends on weather conditions.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in soil or leaf litter, remaining hidden and inactive until spring warmth returns. You won't see them during the cold months.

funFact: Despite being called the 'Japanese' weevil, this little beetle has become such a successful New England resident that it's now more commonly encountered here than many of our native weevil species - a true immigrant success story!
confusionNotes: Other small, dark weevils in gardens might look similar, but the two pale bands across the body are unique to this species. If you can't see clear banding, you're probably looking at a different weevil entirely. Remember: two bands = two-banded Japanese weevil!
contextualKnowledge: Like many insects we call 'Japanese,' this weevil was accidentally introduced from Asia and has adapted remarkably well to New England conditions. It's become a common garden inhabitant without most people even noticing it's there.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other broad-nosed weevils by looking for those distinctive two light bands. Most other weevils in the region either lack banding entirely or have different patterns like spots or mottled coloring rather than clean, straight bands.
